doc.title: Michael Abene interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: Accompanying singers and recent vocal projects
summary: Abene discusses the knack of accompanying singers, knowing standards in many keys, and recent singer projects.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Right. You’ve done a lot of accompanying of vocalists. Is there a special knack that you have to have for that.

Yeah. Steel fortitude for one. Yeah I’ve sort of gotten away from a lot of it. I think playing for a singer is kind of interesting for a pianist, or an arranger, but especially for a pianist. Because I’ve learned a lot of tunes over the years and in any key. So for pianists, if nothing else, just knowing the repertoire of the great American songs, plus being able

to play them in a lot of keys. And so for that it was fun. Obviously for some singers I like playing for and dealing with more than others. But I learned, again, I learned a lot. And also I like writing for singers. I haven’t done so much of that in a while. I did a record for Nnenna Freelon about three years ago called “Maiden Voyage” for Concord and we used different small groups. But generally, this wonderful singer, Jennifer Holliday, who did the original “Dream Girls” cast is a wonderful singer. We just did some symphony stuff for her for a concert in New York. But generally I’ve kind of shied away from that end of it. But I suggest to piano players, because a lot of the young piano players, you say a standard, they think of some 1970’s tune by Wayne Shorter. That to them is a standard. You say no, you don’t understand. It is a standard in a form but I’m talking about Gershwin, Harold Arlen. Because I’ve been doing very little of that kind of stuff, I’ve been doing much more through composed stuff. But I still have fun doing that with the right people. A singer friend of mine just did an album, a dedication to — oh God, isn’t it awful, a wonderful singer too — she did Loch Lomond, isn’t that awful I’m a total blank. Anyways the guys who were on the date — Maxine Sullivan — oh God excuse me. And it was kind of fun. I hadn’t done that kind of music in years but I had guys who had played with her even. I did some gigs years ago, Warren Vache, Michael Hashim on saxophone, James Chirillo the guitarist, Chip Jackson on bass and Dennis Mackrel who was here with the Dizzy band. And it was just kind of a fun thing. But when you get the right players, playing that kind of music, it’s fun. But it’s like I haven’t really just done that kind of a thing. But I enjoyed writing charts for singers. Right now I’m working on a project with Joe Lovano’s wife, Judy Silvano, who is a very good singer. But Judy has always been involved with more free kind of singing and original music. This is an album of standards, although we’re taking the standards very left of center. But it’s not going to be like a lead sheet and we’re going to count off and just play. And we’ve had one rehearsal with some of the guys. Right now Rufus Reid, Billy Hart, Ingrid Jensen is doing it, Dick Oatts on saxophone. So we’re looking to record in May. But we’re taking things kind of, using her voice as an instrument also beside the lyric end of it. I used to love playing for a singer by the name of Sylvia Sims. No chops at all, but swing and great ballads. I love playing ballads for singers more than anything. And also when piano players, a lot of piano players, when they’re playing for singers I feel they play too much. A lot of this, a lot of single note. And I’d just rather play a chord and let it hang. Even when the singer is not singing, just hit a little splank in there, rather than fill up a lot of things. And the other thing I try — I’ve done a lot of workshops, in Europe believe it or not, not as a vocal coach but I certainly can teach phrasing and the main thing I find in most singers, they don’t know how to choose keys.
